tuesday_carousel.caption:
Most brands measure service after the visit.

That is necessary, but incomplete.

In 1980, Richard Oliver described satisfaction as a comparison between expectation and performance. The customer does not simply ask, "Was the service good?" They ask, often silently: "Was this the service I was led to expect?"

That is where many operations lose trust.

A luxury brand can deliver an objectively acceptable experience and still disappoint if the promise was precision. A quick-service brand can create loyalty with something simple if it reliably delivers what it said it would deliver.

This is why I do not like CX programs that only score the frontline. The frontline is not the whole system. Marketing creates expectation. Leadership defines the standard. Operations delivers the proof. Measurement tells us where the chain broke.

The confirmation gap is the distance between the promise and the evidence.

Close that gap and satisfaction stops being opinion. It becomes something you can govern.

Where is your brand promising more than the operation can repeatedly prove?

thursday_post.topic: Field File: The handoff that erased confidence
thursday_post.caption:
Field File: the handoff that erased confidence.

A customer explains the same issue to the first employee. Then again to the supervisor. Then again at the counter.

Nothing dramatic happens. No raised voice. No visible failure. The team is polite.

But the customer has already learned something: the operation does not remember.

That is the kind of service weakness traditional satisfaction scores often miss. The individual interaction can look acceptable while the experience as a system feels careless.

In our work, I pay close attention to repeated explanation. It is one of the cleanest signals that internal handoffs are not governed properly.

Customers rarely describe this as a "process issue." They say, "They were not listening."

That distinction matters.

Because once the customer feels unheard, every next step is interpreted through doubt.

Where in your operation does the customer have to repeat themselves before someone owns the issue?

weekend_reel.caption:
Weekend cut from the CX Series: The Confirmation Gap.

Customer satisfaction is not a raw score. It is a comparison.

What did the customer expect?
What did the operation deliver?
What evidence proves the promise was kept?

That is the gap worth governing.

Where is your operation creating expectation faster than it can deliver proof?
